title: Piedmont
description: At the foot of the Alps: Barolo, Barbaresco and a hillside map as detailed as Burgundy's.
L: At the foot of the mountains
Explain its continental climate and fog

Piedmont, Piemonte, means foot of the mountains. It's in north-west Italy, bordered by the Alps on the north and west and the Apennines to the south. The key wine areas are the Langhe and Roero hills around Alba, and Monferrato around Asti. Piedmont has no IGT wines: everything is DOC or DOCG, with 19 DOCGs.

The mountains create a continental climate: cold winters, hot summers and autumn fog, nebbia, rising from the Tanaro valley. Fog may give Nebbiolo its name. The Alps block cold northern winds, and a rain shadow keeps the region fairly dry. Hail is a risk. Long, cool autumns suit late-ripening grapes.
Piemonte: at the foot of the mountains.

In the Langhe, grape choice follows the slope. The warmest, south-facing slopes, called sorì, go to Nebbiolo, which ripens last. Cooler slopes take Barbera; the coolest, highest sites take Dolcetto or Moscato. This hierarchy is old and practical, and the vineyard landscapes of Langhe-Roero and Monferrato became a UNESCO site in 2014.
Not true. Piedmont has no IGT; its wines are DOC or DOCG.
Piedmont lies at the foot of the Alps, around Alba and Asti
Its continental climate has autumn fog and long ripening
The warmest slopes are kept for Nebbiolo

Nebbiolo makes Barolo, Barbaresco and Roero: pale but powerful, with tar, roses and high tannin. Barbera, the most planted red, gives juicy, high-acid, low-tannin wines. Dolcetto gives soft, dark, early-drinking reds. Other reds include Freisa, Grignolino and Ruchè.

Moscato Bianco makes Asti and Moscato d'Asti, sweet and lightly sparkling. Arneis, revived in the Roero from the 1970s, gives fragrant, pear-scented whites. Cortese makes Gavi, crisp and mineral, in the south-east. Timorasso, near Tortona, is a rising white grape.
Match each grape to its wine.
Each grape has its signature wine.
Langhe Nebbiolo, a DOC, offers Nebbiolo's tar and roses at a much lower price than Barolo, and is ready to drink younger.
Which is Piedmont's most planted red grape?
Barbera covers the most area, though Nebbiolo is the most prestigious.
Nebbiolo, Barbera and Dolcetto lead the reds
Moscato, Arneis and Cortese lead the whites
Barbera is the most planted; Nebbiolo the most prestigious

Barolo DOCG covers 11 villages south-west of Alba. The main ones are Barolo, La Morra, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba. Western villages, on Tortonian marl, like La Morra, give more perfumed, approachable wines. Eastern villages, on Serravallian sandstone and marl, like Serralunga, give more powerful, tannic wines.

Barolo must be 100% Nebbiolo and age at least 38 months, 18 in wood, before release; Riserva at least 62 months. Since 2010, labels can name one of 181 MGAs, Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive, official vineyard areas like Cannubi, Brunate and Rocche dell'Annunziata, similar to Burgundy's crus.
Which part of Barolo gives the most powerful wines?
Serravallian soils in the east give more structure.

From the 1980s, the Barolo wars split producers: modernists used short maceration and new French barriques for softer, fruitier wines; traditionalists kept long maceration and large old casks, botti. Bartolo Mascarello and Giacomo Conterno are traditionalist icons; Elio Altare a modernist. Today, many blend both approaches.
Barolo's 11 villages split into perfumed west and powerful east
It's 100% Nebbiolo, aged at least 38 months

Barbaresco DOCG lies north-east of Alba, near the Tanaro river, mainly in three villages: Barbaresco, Neive and Treiso. It's smaller than Barolo, about 750 hectares compared with about 2,200. It's slightly lower and warmer, closer to the river, so Nebbiolo ripens a little earlier.

Barbaresco must be 100% Nebbiolo, aged at least 26 months, 9 in wood; Riserva 50 months. It has 66 MGAs, like Asili, Rabajà and Montestefano. Its wines are often described as more elegant and approachable earlier than Barolo, with softer tannins, though site and producer matter more.
How does Barbaresco's minimum ageing compare with Barolo's?

Angelo Gaja, from the 1960s, raised Barbaresco's global prestige, with single-vineyard wines and new ideas. The Produttori del Barbaresco, a co-operative founded in 1958, makes some of the best-value fine wines in Italy, including single-vineyard Riservas. Bruno Giacosa was another legend.
Not true. Barbaresco is about a third of Barolo's size.
Barbaresco is smaller, lower and slightly warmer than Barolo
It ages at least 26 months and has 66 MGAs
Gaja and the Produttori raised its prestige

Barbera d'Asti, a DOCG, and Barbera d'Alba, a DOC, are its main wines. Nizza, a DOCG since 2014, is Barbera's top area, in the hills around Nizza Monferrato. Barbera is juicy, high in acidity and low in tannin. Since the 1980s, producers like Giacomo Bologna have aged it in small oak for more structure.

Dolcetto makes soft, dark wines to drink young; Dogliani is its DOCG heartland. Moscato Bianco makes Asti, fully sparkling, and Moscato d'Asti, gently fizzy, frizzante. Both are sweet and low in alcohol: Moscato d'Asti about 5.5%. Fermentation in a sealed tank is stopped by chilling, keeping sugar and bubbles.
Match each wine to its grape.
Piedmont's everyday wines are just as distinctive.
Moscato d'Asti, at 5.5% alcohol and lightly sweet, is a classic with fresh fruit or hazelnut cake, another Piedmont speciality.
How does Moscato d'Asti keep its sweetness and bubbles?
Fermentation in a sealed tank is stopped by chilling
Stopping fermentation keeps sugar; the sealed tank traps CO2.
Barbera d'Asti, Nizza and Barbera d'Alba are juicy, acidic reds
Asti and Moscato d'Asti are sweet and low in alcohol
Reading Piedmont and eating with it

Labels name the DOC or DOCG, like Barolo or Barbera d'Asti, the producer, the vintage and often an MGA or vineyard name. Riserva marks longer ageing. Langhe Nebbiolo and Nebbiolo d'Alba are more affordable Nebbiolos. The DOCG strip on the neck guarantees origin.

Piedmont's food is rich: tajarin, thin egg pasta with butter and white truffle; vitello tonnato; brasato al Barolo, beef braised in Barolo; bagna cauda, a hot garlic and anchovy dip. Barolo suits truffles and braised meat; Barbera suits salumi and pasta; Dolcetto suits everyday dishes; Moscato suits hazelnut cake.
Truffle with Barolo, salumi with Barbera
Which Piedmont dish is cooked with Barolo?

Serve Barolo and Barbaresco at 17 to 18 degrees, in large glasses, decanted for hours when young. They're best from 10 years and can age 30 or more. Barbera and Dolcetto at 15 to 17, young. Moscato d'Asti well chilled, at 6 to 8.
Sorbet is too sweet and acidic.
Labels show DOCG, MGA and Riserva
Barolo suits truffle and braised beef; Barbera suits salumi
Decant young Barolo; it ages 30 years or more
Match each wine to its rule.
Which slopes are reserved for Nebbiolo?
Nebbiolo ripens last and needs the best sites.
Piedmont's official vineyard areas in Barolo are called ____.
Piedmont is foggy, hilly and all DOC or DOCG
Nebbiolo makes Barolo and Barbaresco on the best slopes
Barbera, Dolcetto and Moscato make everyday wines
Its rich food, from truffle to brasato, suits its wines
